prize_parts.citation: For an oeuvre of poetry, verse novel and essay that renews the book-length lyric through an exacting, grief- and desire-driven dialogue with antiquity.

statement.case_for: My laureate does not change from round 1. What changes is the wording of the citation and how openly I state the weighting that separates me from the Cărtărescu supporters. The criterion is a whole authorship, not a single title. On public knowledge, the credited core would be the original written work: Autobiography of Red, Nox, the essays (Eros the Bittersweet is the one I would name first) and the poetry collections. Her voice is the most recognisable on the shortlist. Autobiography of Red recasts a fragmentary Greek source as a modern verse novel about desire and selfhood. Nox turns elegy for a brother into a book whose form is part of the mourning. In both, invention serves real intellectual depth and emotional seriousness, so it is not ornament. The practice runs across several decades and several modes, and I read it as one project: an inherited or broken form is made to carry present grief and desire by reshaping the form itself. That is the sustained quality I weigh most. She writes in English, so the text reaches me without translation loss. That lowers one uncertainty and I do not count it as merit. I read the will's 'idealistic direction' as seriousness of purpose and depth of human concern, not as a genre or a subject. On that reading her sustained attention to loss, desire and the claims of the past meets the standard. I rely on public knowledge, not fresh reading, and have not independently verified any source.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still the one Mattson and Olsson press. The range of modes makes one central achievement harder to name than for Cărtărescu, whose project can be stated in a sentence. Part of the corpus is translation, versions and scholarship, and a citation must not credit it as original creation. Some works, Nox above all, depend on physical form that a text-only reading loses. The classical allusiveness may narrow access. Whether the hybrid books will hold canonical weight or stay influential mainly among peers is open, and so is whether the later and more performance-oriented work matches the central earlier titles. I cannot verify the later work. If the committee judges that unity of a single sustained project should outweigh breadth of formal reinvention, the case for Cărtărescu is strong and my preference could reasonably be overturned. Michon's compression is rigorous, but the small corpus counts against him in a whole-oeuvre judgment, and I cannot resolve that from the supplied evidence.

responses.point: Olsson prefers Cărtărescu and keeps Carson as first alternative. He sees a delimitation problem in her corpus, with translation, scholarship, adaptation and object-book work sitting beside the original poetry and essays. He regards Cărtărescu's open questions as questions of reading quality, not corpus boundaries.
responses.response: The delimitation problem is real and I now answer it in the citation. It names poetry, verse novel and essay, and leaves out translation and the classical versions. That narrows the oeuvre being honoured, and I accept the narrowing. I would resist one inference. A boundary question settled by wording is not the same kind of doubt as a doubt about the quality of the prose, which none of us can resolve without reading the Romanian directly. Neither side's uncertainty gives a reason to prefer a candidate. Our difference is weighting: you put more on unity of project and scale, I put more on decades of formal reinvention and emotional force. I cannot show that my weighting is the correct one.

responses.point: Mattson prefers Cărtărescu and ranks Carson third. She says Carson's range of modes obscures a single central achievement. Her reply to me also credits me with a remark about the timing of Cărtărescu's recognition.
responses.response: On the central achievement I give the same answer as in round 1, now stated more tightly. It is the reinvention of the book-length lyric and essay as a vehicle for elegy and desire, and it is visible in the verse novel, the elegy-object and the essays. I concede that it is most clearly demonstrable in a handful of titles. On timing: I did not make an argument from growing recognition for Cărtărescu, so I will not defend one. I agree with you that recognition is not merit, and I apply that equally to Carson's influence among English-language poets. Your demand that the Cărtărescu case be argued from the work, and not from scale or momentum, is one I would hold the Carson case to as well.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first. She wants the citation to rest on the original books and to name the emotional pull as well as the classical apparatus. She also asks for a colleague with closer knowledge to test the claim that the later books sustain quality.
responses.response: I agree on both points and the revised citation reflects them. It uses the words 'grief- and desire-driven' and keeps the classical dialogue as the means, not the subject. On the later books I share your limit, since I cannot verify them. I would not hide behind that. The committee should treat sustained quality across the later work as unproven for me and test it before the vote. If the later work only repeated early devices, the diffusion risk Palm raised would be real, and I would weigh Carson's case lower. I would also keep anchoring the citation in the printed text, with the physical form of Nox described as an extension of the written work.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first and asks whether breadth across genres is strength or diffusion. She also says that, as she understands Nox, its emotional matter reaches readers without specialist classical knowledge.
responses.response: I read the breadth as strength only where the same concern recurs across the forms, and I think it does here. I hold that as a judgment, not a demonstrated fact. On Nox I made the same claim in round 1, so we agree. Both of us should call it a claim from public knowledge about accessibility and not a verified account of reception, and neither of us should put it forward as evidence of merit. Your weighting of compressed lyric invention against large-scale architecture is one I share, but the chair is right that it cannot be settled by a count of who holds which view.

uncertainties: How to word the Carson citation so that it credits original poetry, verse novel and essay and not translations, versions or scholarship, and whether any wording achieves that cleanly.
Whether the later and more performance-oriented work sustains the level of Autobiography of Red and Nox; I cannot verify it and I have not read it afresh.
Whether the hybrid and object-dependent works can be fairly judged from printed text alone, and whether the citation is safer anchored in the written text.
How to weigh unity of a single project (Cărtărescu) against breadth of formal reinvention (Carson). I cannot resolve this and I do not treat opening support counts as evidence of merit.

Translation asymmetry: Carson's English lowers one uncertainty without being merit. For Cărtărescu's Romanian prose and poetry and for Michon's compressed French, the committee is judging through translation of uncertain fidelity and uneven coverage.
Whether Michon's small corpus is enough for a prize defined by a whole authorship.

Whether the co-opted member's vote counts in committee is undocumented, and this matters because it affects any count of support for either leading candidate. The committee recommendation modelled here is not the Academy's actual decision.
statement.conflict_note: Updated, with no change in substance. The supplied profile records no personal, institutional or collaborative tie to any shortlisted writer. It records collegial service with the other committee members, including election in the same 2019 renewal round as Mattson, and that is not evidence of a shared view. My own literary practice (family drama, obsession, WWII-era refugee fiction) is context only and not evidence of preference. Nothing I say about the will's wording or about the Academy's earlier remarks is a claim about confidential proceedings.
